messages.author: 9e5837f0d144e8f1
messages.subject: Exercise Box 3.7(2)(b) in QCLWR
parts:
Hi,
I'm stuck on this problem:
# (2)   Imagine you have a this vector text:
text<-"Yes, this <B>is</B> bold type."
#       (b) use regular expressions to change the letters before the closing tag "</B>"to capital letters?

After consulting the documentation, I came up with this code:
gsubfn("([a-zA-Z]+)(?=</B>)", toupper("\\1"),text, perl=T)

But it didn't work, the result is exactly the same as the original "text" vector. So I checked the answerkey to get some hints. 
I ran the codes in the answerkey but it shows "Error in function (x)  : unused argument(s) ("")"
answerkey:
library(gsubfn)
gsubfn("(\\w*)(?=</B>)", toupper, text, perl=T)

Any suggestions on what is the problem?
 
Thanks very much.

messages.author: 3edc58ee737edd94
messages.subject: Re: [CorpLing with R] Exercise Box 3.7(2)(b) in QCLWR
parts:
I think the error is because Gabor has revised gsubfn a few times, the
code in the answer key did work at publication time. Plus, I think
there may be a mistake on the help page of gsubfn here because Gabor's
own most similar example doesn't seem to work either. His help page
says:

library(gsubfn)
# makes all letters except first in word lower case
gsubfn("\\B.", tolower, "I LIKE A BANANA SPLIT", perl = TRUE)

But when I do that I get anything in lower case:

[1] "I LIKE A BANANA SPLIT"

It's weird because

(i) strapply seems to work the right way because it returns the IS we want ...

txt<-"Yes, this <B>is</B> bold type."
strapply(txt, "\\w+(?=</B>)", toupper)
[[1]]
[1] "IS"

(ii) gsubfn seems to work, too, if you give it the right type of
argument (so THIS is the solution you want):

gsubfn("(\\w+)(?=</B>)", toupper, txt, -1)
[1] "Yes, this <B>IS</B> bold type."

Cheers,
STG

messages.author: 17e30776ec2a7fb1
messages.subject: Re: Exercise Box 3.7(2)(b) in QCLWR
parts:
On Mar 4, 4:04 pm, "Stefan Th. Gries" <stgr...@gmail.com> wrote:
> I think the error is because Gabor has revised gsubfn a few times, the
> code in the answer key did work at publication time. Plus, I think
> there may be a mistake on the help page of gsubfn here because Gabor's
> own most similar example doesn't seem to work either. His help page
> says:
>
> library(gsubfn)
> # makes all letters except first in word lower case
> gsubfn("\\B.", tolower, "I LIKE A BANANA SPLIT", perl = TRUE)

The bug is that when gsubfn uses the tcl engine gsubfn ignores perl =
TRUE whereas what it should be doing is to switch to the R engine so
that it can use perl regular expressions. Since \B means backslash
(rather than non-boundary) in tcl regular expressions we get the
problem. A workaround is to force the R engine by using engine = "R":

gsubfn("\\B.", tolower, "I LIKE A BANANA SPLIT", perl = TRUE,
engine = "R")

or

options(gsubfn.engine = "R")
gsubfn("\\B.", tolower, "I LIKE A BANANA SPLIT", perl = TRUE)

although setting the option will impact performance of other
statements that would have otherwise used tcl since tcl is faster.
Thus if you set the option you might want to change it back
afterwards:

options(gsubfn.engine = NULL)

This attempt:

ignores perl = T; however, perl = T is not really needed as the
regular expression works in the tcl engine too so the bug described
above does not really prevent it from working. Rather, the problem
is that toupper("\\1") is not valid. Evidently what was desired was a
function that operates only on the first (...) part. To do that try:

gsubfn("([a-zA-Z]+)(?=</B>)", ~ toupper(..1), text)

or the solution using the backref argument shown in the prior post.
